opus-5.5.text:
I think we're in a really interesting but also somewhat early phase. When we started working on the AI Scientist, the goal was to see whether you could close the full loop: generate an idea, write the code, run the experiments, analyze the results, and write it up as a paper. It turned out you can, at least in constrained settings. But "can do the loop" is very different from "can do the loop independently and produce something genuinely valuable."

Right now these systems are good at local exploration. Given a codebase and a template, they can try variations, find small improvements, and document them reasonably well. What they're still weak at is taste: knowing which questions matter, recognizing when a result is surprising versus just a bug, and deciding when to abandon a direction. A lot of scientific progress comes from that kind of judgment, and it's hard to specify as an objective.

There's also the verification problem. In machine learning we're relatively lucky because experiments are cheap and the feedback loop is fast. You can run code and get a number. In wet-lab biology or physics, the system has to interact with the real world, which is slower, more expensive, and noisier. So I'd expect independence to come first in computational fields and much later elsewhere.

That said, I don't think the right framing is a binary of human-dependent versus fully independent. What I find more likely, and honestly more exciting in the near term, is a gradual shift in where the human sits. Today the human sets the template, picks the problem, and filters the outputs. Over time I'd expect the human to move up a level: setting broader research agendas, curating which directions get compute, and acting more like a PI overseeing many automated students. The open-endedness angle matters here too. If you want systems that keep discovering interesting things without a human constantly steering, you need some notion of interestingness and novelty that the system can pursue on its own. That's a deep, unsolved research problem, and it's one I care a lot about.

And then there are the responsibility questions. If these systems produce papers at scale, how do we review them? How do we prevent flooding the literature with plausible-looking but shallow work? We tried to be transparent about this, including being explicit when AI-generated work went through review. I think the community needs norms around disclosure and evaluation before we hand over too much autonomy.

So my short answer: technically, more autonomy is coming faster than many people expect, especially in computational science. But meaningful independence, where the system decides what's worth knowing and reliably judges its own results, is still a significant leap. For the foreseeable future I see it as a powerful amplifier of human scientists rather than a replacement.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about what "independent" means here. If you mean fully autonomous systems that pick their own research directions, run experiments, and publish without any human in the loop, I'm quite skeptical that's close, and honestly I'm not sure it's desirable. If you mean systems that can take a reasonably well-scoped problem and run a large part of the pipeline themselves, from hypothesis generation through experiment design, code, analysis, and a write-up, then I think we're already there for narrow slices, and the question is how far that envelope expands.

From our experience building the AI Scientist at Sakana, the pieces that work well today are the mechanical ones. Writing a baseline, modifying it, running sweeps, producing plots, drafting a paper in a template. Those are tasks where you can define success and iterate cheaply. What's much harder is taste. Knowing which of a thousand plausible ideas is actually worth spending compute on, recognizing when a result is interesting rather than merely non-null, and noticing when something has gone subtly wrong in the setup. Models are getting better at this, but a lot of what we see is still pattern-matching on what papers look like rather than genuine scientific judgment.

There are also a few structural bottlenecks that people underestimate. The first is evaluation. If you want a system to improve itself as a researcher, you need a reward signal, and peer review is slow, noisy, and gameable. We've seen the system produce papers that got through a workshop review, but that says as much about review as about the science. The second is the physical world. In machine learning you can close the loop entirely in silicon, which is why this field is the testbed. In biology or materials you hit wet lab throughput, and automation there is improving but is nowhere near the iteration speed that makes these systems compelling. The third is that science isn't just producing results, it's a social process. Deciding what matters, what to trust, and what to build on is done by a community, and I don't see that being delegated to a model soon.

So my honest assessment is a gradual shift in the division of labor rather than a sudden handoff. Humans move up the stack, setting agendas, asking the right questions, and sanity-checking, while systems do more of the execution and increasingly more of the ideation. I'd guess within a few years a meaningful fraction of empirical ML papers will have most of their experimental work done by agents. Whether that counts as independence depends on how much you value the part humans still do, and I'd argue that's the most important part. I'd also add that we should want to keep it that way for a while. Research that nobody understands or has validated isn't really knowledge yet, and the credibility of the whole enterprise depends on that human loop staying in place, even as it gets thinner.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by independent. There’s a difference between a system that can carry out an experiment without supervision and one that can decide which scientific questions are worth pursuing.

You can imagine automating a lot of the research loop: proposing a hypothesis, writing code, running experiments, analyzing the results, and using those results to propose the next experiment. That seems particularly plausible in domains where experiments are cheap and feedback is relatively clear. But a system can go through all those steps and still be optimizing a poorly chosen objective. Producing a convincing paper isn’t necessarily the same thing as producing reliable new knowledge.

So I’d look at whether these systems can recognize when their assumptions are wrong, design experiments that challenge their own explanations, and produce results that survive independent scrutiny. Those are more meaningful milestones than how long they can run unattended.

My expectation is that independence will be gradual and uneven. We’ll delegate increasingly large parts of research, while humans continue to shape the questions and judge the significance of the answers. Whether that eventually becomes something more autonomous is an open question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by independent. There’s a difference between a system that can carry out an experiment without supervision and one that can decide which scientific questions are worth pursuing. You can imagine automating quite a lot of the loop: proposing hypotheses, writing code, running experiments, and using the results to choose the next experiment. But that loop can still sit inside a problem formulation supplied by a human.

The harder question is whether these systems can recognize when the formulation itself is wrong. Are we measuring the right thing? Is an apparently positive result actually an artifact of the evaluation? Running more experiments doesn’t necessarily resolve those questions, especially if the system is also designing its own tests.

So I’m optimistic about increasingly autonomous research within well-defined environments, particularly where feedback is cheap and reliable. I’m more uncertain about open-ended scientific independence. I’d expect human involvement to shift toward choosing objectives and scrutinizing evidence, rather than disappear all at once.
